title: Buying a Home With Student Loans: What Lenders Look At
description: Student loans don't disqualify you from buying a home. Learn how lenders count student loan payments under deferred and income-driven plans and how to plan.
keywords: buying a house with student loans
image_alt: A man holding a card while looking at his laptop

faq.q: Can I buy a house if I have student loans?
faq.a: Yes. Many buyers have student loans. What matters is how the monthly payment affects your debt-to-income ratio and whether the overall picture fits the loan program.

faq.q: How do lenders count deferred student loans?
faq.a: It depends on the program. Some use a calculated payment based on a percentage of the balance, while others may use a documented payment amount. Your loan officer can tell you which rule applies.

faq.q: Does an income-driven repayment plan help me qualify?
faq.a: Often, yes. Many programs allow the documented income-driven payment to be used, which can be lower than a standard payment. Rules vary by loan type.

body_html:
If you have student loans, you're far from alone, and you're not locked out of homeownership. Many of my first-time buyers carry student debt. The question isn't whether you have it; it's how the payment fits into the rest of your finances and how your specific loan program counts it.

Why student loans matter to lenders

Lenders care about your debt-to-income ratio: your monthly debts, including the new housing payment, compared with your gross monthly income. Student loan payments are part of that calculation. A higher student loan payment leaves less room for a housing payment, which can affect how much you qualify for.

How the payment gets counted

This is where it gets technical, because rules differ by loan program.

SituationHow it's often handled
Standard repaymentThe actual monthly payment on your credit report or statement
Income-driven repaymentMany programs accept the documented payment, even if lower
Deferment or forbearanceOften a calculated payment based on a percentage of the balance, depending on the program
A payment of zero under an income-driven planSome programs accept it with documentation; others use a calculated amount

Because conventional, FHA, and VA loans each have their own rules, the same borrower can qualify differently depending on the program. That's one of the best reasons to have a loan officer compare options before you start house hunting.

Documentation to gather

  • A recent statement from your servicer showing the balance and required monthly payment
  • Proof of your income-driven repayment plan, if applicable
  • Documentation of any deferment or forbearance status and end date
  • Information on any loans in collections or default, which need to be addressed

Make sure your credit report matches your servicer's records. Mismatches between the two are a common source of delays.

Strategies that can help

  1. Enroll in an income-driven plan, if it fits your long-term goals. A lower documented payment can improve your ratio. Consider the long-term cost and any forgiveness implications first.
  2. Pay down other debts. Eliminating a car payment or credit card balance can offset a student loan payment.
  3. Compare programs. One program's calculation may work better than another's for your situation.
  4. Add a co-borrower. A spouse or partner with qualifying income can strengthen the application.
  5. Adjust your target price. Sometimes a slightly lower price point makes everything fit comfortably.

What about loans in default?

Federal student loans in default or collections can be a serious obstacle, particularly for government-backed loans like FHA and VA. If you have a defaulted loan, talk to your servicer about rehabilitation or consolidation options well before applying, and loop in your loan officer so you understand how each path affects your timeline.

Don't forget the bigger picture

Qualifying is one thing. Feeling comfortable is another. Build a budget that includes your student loan payment, the full housing payment, retirement savings, and an emergency fund. If the numbers only work by stretching, it may be worth waiting a little longer or choosing a lower price point.

Student loans are part of your financial picture, not a barrier to it. The key is knowing how your program counts them.

Plan ahead with your loan officer

The best time to talk about student loans is months before you want to buy. Repayment plan changes, payoff strategies, and credit improvements all take time to show up. A quick review now can save you from surprises later and help you decide which program fits best. My first-time homebuyer roadmap shows where this fits in the bigger process.

Public Service Loan Forgiveness and homebuying

If you work in public service and are pursuing loan forgiveness, buying a home doesn't have to derail your plan. The key is understanding how your required payment is documented and counted. Borrowers on income-driven plans should keep their recertification current, because an expired certification can cause the servicer to show a much higher payment. That higher number can suddenly appear on your credit report right when you're applying.

Before you apply, log in to your servicer account and confirm three things: your current plan, your required monthly payment, and the date your next recertification is due. Download a statement showing all three. It's a small step that prevents one of the most common last-minute surprises I see.

Married borrowers and student loans

When both spouses apply, both sets of student loans count toward the combined ratio. When only one spouse applies, generally only that person's debts are counted, though rules can vary by program and state. Some couples find that applying with one income works better; others need both incomes to qualify. Run both scenarios with your loan officer before deciding, and remember that title and loan decisions can have legal implications worth discussing with a professional.

  • Applying jointly combines both incomes and both debts
  • Applying individually uses only one income and that person's debts
  • The better structure depends on the numbers, so compare both

A quick pre-application checklist

  • Download your latest servicer statement showing balance and required payment
  • Confirm your repayment plan and recertification date
  • Compare your servicer's figures with your credit report
  • Resolve any defaulted or collection accounts
  • Ask your loan officer which program counts your loans most favorably

The takeaway

You can absolutely buy a home with student loans. Know your payment, understand how your loan program counts it, gather clean documentation, and compare options. With a little planning, your student debt becomes just one more line in a budget that works.
